news.title: Windows Update Is Breaking Printers and PDFs — Here's What to Do
news.excerpt: Microsoft's latest Windows update is breaking printers and PDF saving across the country. Programs crash when you try to print or create a PDF. Here is what to do right now: open Settings, go to Windows Update, and click "Pause updates" for 7 days. If your printer already stopped working, try printing from a web browser instead. This is a Microsoft mistake, not a printer problem. They are working on a fix. Bring it by the shop if you need help — free diagnosis, no pressure. (Sources: PCWorld, BleepingComputer — August 25-26, 2026)

news.title: Fake Email Attachments Are Stealing Microsoft 365 Logins — Even With Two-Factor On
news.excerpt: Security researchers found a new trick hitting over 4,500 companies across the U.S. Crooks send emails with attachments that look like a Microsoft login page. When you open the attachment, it loads a fake sign-in screen and steals your username, password, and even your two-factor code — all in one shot. The attackers then reuse your login session without needing your password again. The FTC says never open unexpected email attachments, even if they look official. If you get a surprise attachment asking you to "verify" your account, delete it and go directly to outlook.com or office.com instead (The Hacker News, August 25; CybersecurityNews, August 26).

news.title: Fake Ads on Social Media Are Trapping Shoppers — FTC Warns
news.excerpt: The Federal Trade Commission warns that ads on social media platforms are not checked for scams. Crooks run fake ads on Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok using stolen product photos and made-up reviews — you pay but the item never arrives, or it shows up broken. The FTC says this happens every day and costs people real money (FTC.gov, August 2026). Before buying from any social media ad, search the company name plus "scam" on Google. If the company has no real website or phone number, don't buy. Always use a credit card so you can dispute the charge.

news.title: Fake Postcards Promise VA Benefits — It's a Scam Stealing Veterans' Personal Info
news.excerpt: Scammers are mailing official-looking postcards to veterans across the country, promising free monthly VA benefit payments. The postcard includes a phone number and website asking for your Social Security number or bank details to "verify eligibility." The real VA never contacts veterans this way — they already have your information on file. If you or a loved one receives one of these postcards, do not call the number or visit the website. Instead, verify any VA communication through va.gov or call 1-800-827-1000 directly. Report the scam to ReportFraud.ftc.gov. — Source: FTC, August 24, 2026

news.title: Brushing Scams: Why Random Packages Are Showing Up at Your Door
news.excerpt: A package shows up on your porch you never ordered. The FTC warned on August 20 that this is a "brushing" scam — sellers send you free junk using your name so they can post a fake five-star review in your name. Some packages include QR codes that lead to fake websites designed to steal your information. If you receive a package you did not order, do not scan any codes inside. Check your online accounts for unfamiliar orders and report it free at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

posts.title: CISA says hackers are already using six new flaws — update your computer tonight and tell your IT department if you use Citrix at work
posts.summary: The government's cybersecurity agency (CISA) added six newly exploited vulnerabilities to its catalog on August 26 — including a Citrix flaw that lets hackers break into remote access systems without a password. If your company uses Citrix for remote work, tell your IT department to patch it tonight. On your own computer, press Start, type "check for updates," open Windows Update, and install whatever is available. It takes two minutes.
posts.truth: I see this all the time — businesses assume their IT person handles updates and they don't need to worry about it. But CISA's alert specifically says these flaws are being actively exploited right now, not someday. If your company uses Citrix for remote access, the clock is ticking. And if you're a home user, keeping your Windows updates current is still the single fastest way to stay safe. Most people don't realize that a two-minute update once a month can stop a hacker cold.

posts.title: Google's free Password Checkup finds every weak and reused password in Chrome — try it in 10 seconds
posts.summary: Open Chrome, click your profile icon in the top right, select "Google Password Manager," then click "Password Checkup." Google will scan every password saved in your browser and tell you which ones are weak, reused, or leaked in a data breach — for free, in about 10 seconds.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that if you use the same password for your email and your bank — which about 65% of people do — a single data breach at some website you signed up for three years ago can hand a crook access to everything. Google's Password Checkup shows you exactly which passwords are in danger, and it takes less time than filling your coffee mug. I run this on every computer that comes into the shop.

posts.title: Turn any lamp into a smart lamp for 10 dollars — TP-Link Kasa Smart Plug lets you control it from your phone with the free Kasa app
posts.summary: Buy a TP-Link Kasa Smart Plug EP25 for about 10 dollars at Amazon or Walmart, plug it into any wall outlet, plug in your lamp, and control it from the free Kasa Smart app on your phone — set schedules, turn lights on from bed, or flip them off from the grocery store.
posts.truth: I see people spend 200 dollars on "smart home" systems when all they really want is to turn the porch light on before they get home. A 10-dollar smart plug does that. You don't need a hub, you don't need a subscription, and you don't need to call me. Download the free Kasa Smart app from the Play Store or App Store, follow the 2-minute setup, and you're done. I put one on my mom's lamp so she can turn it on without getting up — she thinks it's magic.

posts.title: Windows 11 August update causes games to crash and PCs to reboot — Microsoft is working on a patch
posts.summary: If your PC crashes, freezes, or reboots by itself after the August Windows update, you're not alone — Microsoft has confirmed the issue and a proper fix is on the way. Don't uninstall the update, which leaves you vulnerable to 400+ security holes; just wait for Microsoft's patch within the next few weeks.
posts.truth: I've been seeing this all week in the shop — customers come in thinking their PC is dying, but it's actually the August update conflicting with an old RGB lighting driver. The problem is real but temporary. Microsoft's proper patch should arrive soon, and in the meantime the affected games and apps still work fine on most PCs. The only people who should be worried are folks who rely on specific gaming software for work.

posts.title: CISA Flags 4 Actively Exploited Flaws — Update Your Mac and Windows Now
posts.summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added four new actively exploited vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on August 18. Two affect Apple Macs and two affect Windows. Update macOS at System Settings > General > Software Update and Windows at Settings > Windows Update tonight.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that when CISA adds a flaw to its "Known Exploited Vulnerabilities" list, it means hackers are already using it right now — not someday, not theoretically, right now. The Apple macOS flaw lets someone on your network authenticate to your Mac's screen sharing without proper credentials. On Windows, a flaw in a core networking service could let an attacker take over your computer with admin-level control. I see this all the time: customers come in two weeks after an alert saying "I thought it was fine." By then the damage is done. The honest answer is: if your computer is on and connected to the internet, you need to update it tonight.

posts.title: Stop losing things you copied — Windows Clipboard History remembers your last 25 clips, built-in and free
posts.summary: Press the Windows key + V to open Windows Clipboard History. It remembers everything you copy — text, links, images — and lets you paste any older item, not just the most recent one. If it's not turned on yet, press Start, type "clipboard settings," open it, and flip the switch to On. It takes five seconds and you'll never lose a copied item again.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that when you copy something new on your computer, the old thing you copied disappears. Windows Clipboard History fixes that — it keeps your last 25 copies so you can go back and paste any of them. I use it ten times a day when I'm juggling parts numbers, customer notes, and URLs. It's the most underused free tool in Windows.

posts.title: Rapid Fiber just finished wiring every SVEC member in Columbia County — check plans from 50 dollars a month at rapid-fiber.com
posts.summary: Rapid Fiber Internet, powered by Suwannee Valley Electric Cooperative, has completed its initial fiber build — every SVEC member in Columbia County, Suwannee, Lafayette, and Hamilton counties can now get fiber internet. Plans start at 50 dollars a month for 100 Mbps. Check your address and sign up at rapid-fiber.com or call (888) 857-4959.
posts.truth: I've been watching Rapid Fiber roll out for almost three years, and they finally hit 100% coverage for SVEC members. Most people in this area have been stuck with slow DSL or spotty satellite while the rest of the country moved to fiber. This is real gigabit-speed internet through your electric co-op — and it means you finally have an option if Xfinity or AT&T don't reach your road. If you're an SVEC member, you need to check this today.

posts.title: Can't read the small text on your computer screen? Windows Magnifier makes everything bigger free — press the Windows key and Plus to zoom in instantly
posts.summary: Press the Windows key and the Plus sign (+) to zoom in on anything on your screen, press Windows key and Minus to zoom back out, and press Windows key and Escape to turn Magnifier off — built into every Windows 10 and 11 computer, no download needed.
posts.truth: I can't tell you how many customers come in thinking they need a new monitor because the text is too small. They don't — they just need Magnifier. It's been built into Windows for years and almost nobody knows it exists. Press Windows key + Plus and your entire screen zooms in. You can even choose a lens mode that works like a magnifying glass that follows your mouse around the screen.

posts.title: Chrome 153 ships with a critical security patch — take 30 seconds to update now
posts.summary: Open Chrome, click the three dots at top right, click Help, then About Google Chrome — the update installs automatically when you open that page.
posts.truth: Google just patched a critical memory bug in Chrome 153 that could let a bad website take over your computer. The update is free, takes 30 seconds, and you don't need to do anything except open the update page. I check this for every customer who comes in — it's one of the fastest ways to stay safe online. Most people don't realize their browser is the front door to their computer, and keeping it updated is the easiest protection you have.

posts.title: Patch My PC Home Updater Updates 500 Apps Free at patchmypc.com
posts.summary: Download Patch My PC Home Updater free at patchmypc.com, run it, and click Scan — it finds every outdated app on your PC and updates them all in one click. It supports over 500 apps including Chrome, Firefox, Zoom, VLC, 7-Zip, iTunes, Skype, and more.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that old versions of programs are the #1 way hackers get into your computer. Every outdated app is an open door. I see this all the time: customers have the same version of Chrome from six months ago, or their Zoom is three updates behind. The honest answer is: nobody wants to sit there updating 15 apps one by one. Patch My PC solves that. You download it once, run it, and it handles everything. It is not installed permanently — it runs like a quick checkup tool. I use it in the shop on every machine that comes through.
